# React Style

Conventions for writing React components and hooks in this project. General TypeScript rules live in `typescript.md`.

## Call hooks only at the top level of a component or custom hook

_high · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Call every hook unconditionally at the top level of a function component or a custom hook, before any early return. Put the condition inside the hook's callback or below the hook call instead.

**Why.** React matches hook state by call order, so a hook that runs only on some renders shifts every later hook onto the wrong state or crashes with "Rendered fewer hooks than expected"; the React Compiler also skips such a component and leaves it unoptimized.

**Correct:**

```tsx
function Profile({ userId }: ProfileProps) {
  const [tab, setTab] = React.useState<Tab>("posts");
  if (!userId) {
    return null;
  }
  return <Tabs value={tab} onChange={setTab} />;
}
```

**Exceptions.** `React.use` may be called inside conditions and loops; it still must not be called inside a `try`/`catch` block.

## Adopt the React Compiler and stop hand-writing memoization

_high · typescript, react, react-compiler_

**Decision.** Run the React Compiler on the whole app (`compilationMode: "infer"`, the default) and write components as plain code: no `useMemo`, `useCallback` or `memo` except the four documented cases (a callback for a non-React library, a context provider value, a measured expensive computation, a subscription handler), each with a JSDoc comment. Lint with the `recommended` preset of `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`, which carries the compiler rules, and fix what it reports instead of disabling rules. Call hooks only at the top level, since the compiler skips code that breaks the Rules of Hooks.

### Options

| Option | Fits when | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `reactCompiler: true` (infer mode, all components) | new code, or an app whose lint is clean | slightly slower builds; components that break the rules are skipped silently unless linted |
| `reactCompiler: { compilationMode: "annotation" }` with `"use memo"` per component | a large legacy app adopted one module at a time | every component must be opted in by hand; easy to forget |
| compiler off | the app cannot install the Babel plugin | every memoization is manual and its dependency arrays drift |

`"use no memo"` inside a component opts it out. Use it only as a temporary escape hatch for a component that misbehaves when compiled, with a JSDoc comment naming the bug, and remove it once the code is fixed.

`reactCompiler.environment.enablePreserveExistingMemoizationGuarantees` decides whether the compiler keeps the guarantees of `useMemo`/`useCallback` already in the code. Its default differs between compiler versions, so set it explicitly when you rely on it.

### Evolution

**Enable it (Next.js 16).** Install `babel-plugin-react-compiler` as a dev dependency and set the top-level `reactCompiler: true` in `next.config.ts`. Before Next.js 16 the key was `experimental.reactCompiler`; move it when upgrading. Outside Next.js, add the Babel plugin first in the plugin list.

**Lint it.** Install `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` and add `reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended` to `eslint.config.js`. It replaces the older `eslint-plugin-react-compiler`; remove that plugin and its `react-compiler/react-compiler` rule. `preserve-manual-memoization` checks that memoization already in the code can be kept by the compiler; it does not flag memoization as unnecessary.

**Verify it is active.** In development, React DevTools shows a "Memo ✨" badge next to compiled components. In build output, compiled modules import `react/compiler-runtime`. A component without the badge was skipped: read the lint output for it.

**Migrate one module at a time.**

1. Fix the lint diagnostics in the module so the compiler stops skipping its components.
2. Remove `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` from it.
3. Keep only the four exception cases and add the JSDoc comment that names each.
4. Run the module's tests and stories, then move to the next module.

**Profile before adding memoization back.** Record the interaction in the React DevTools Profiler, or wrap the subtree in `<React.Profiler id="..." onRender={...}>` and send the durations to the project logger or a test assertion. Add manual memoization only when the profile shows a component rendering more than about 10 times a second, a render over 16 ms, or a computation over 100 ms, and write the measured figure in its JSDoc comment.

## Key list items by a stable id from the data, never by the array index

_high · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Give each element rendered in `map` a `key` taken from the data: an `id`, a slug or another unique field. When the data has none, attach a generated id when the data is created or loaded, not while rendering.

**Why.** With index keys, reordering, filtering or inserting rows makes React reuse the wrong component, so a row keeps another row's input text or open state; a key generated during render (`crypto.randomUUID()` inside `map`) is worse, because it remounts every row on every render.

**Correct:**

```tsx
function TodoList({ todos }: TodoListProps) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map((todo) => (
        <TodoItem key={todo.id} todo={todo} />
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

## Leave memoization to the React Compiler; memoize by hand only in four documented cases

_high · typescript, react, react-compiler_

**Rule.** Write derived values, event handlers and components as plain code and let the React Compiler memoize them. Do not add `React.useMemo`, `React.useCallback` or `React.memo` unless the case is one of the four exceptions below, and then put a JSDoc comment on it that names the exception.

**Why.** Hand-written memoization in compiled code is noise with dependency arrays that drift out of date, so a stale `useCallback` quietly keeps calling an old prop; the compiler already memoizes the same values with correct dependencies.

**Correct:**

```tsx
function ProductList({ products, sortBy, onSelect }: ProductListProps) {
  const sorted = [...products].sort(byField(sortBy));
  return <List items={sorted} onSelect={(id) => onSelect(id)} />;
}
```

**Exceptions.** Memoize by hand, with a JSDoc comment stating which case applies, only for:

1. **A callback handed to code outside React** (a map, chart or editor library that keeps the reference): `/** Stable reference: the map library re-binds its click handler when this changes. */`
2. **A context provider value** that is an object or function, so consumers do not re-render on every provider render: `/** Context value: keeps every consumer from re-rendering when the provider does. */`
3. **A computation measured as expensive** in the React Profiler (a render over 16 ms, or a computation over 100 ms that runs often): `/** Measured: ~150 ms for 10k rows in the Profiler. */`
4. **A subscription handler** passed to an effect that subscribes to an external store or socket, so it does not resubscribe on every render: `/** Stable handler: prevents resubscribing to the channel on every render. */`

## Render conditionally with a ternary that returns null, never with &&

_high · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Write every conditional in JSX as `condition ? <Element /> : null`, including fragments and inline text. Do not use the `&&` short-circuit.

**Why.** With `&&`, a falsy non-boolean left side such as `0` or `""` is rendered as-is, so an empty list shows a stray "0" on the page; the ternary always renders exactly the element or nothing.

**Correct:**

```tsx
function OrderList({ orders, error }: OrderListProps) {
  return (
    <section>
      {orders.length > 0 ? <List items={orders} /> : null}
      {error ? <p className="text-error">{error}</p> : null}
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Ship every component with a stories file beside it

_medium · typescript, react, storybook_

**Rule.** Create `{component}.stories.tsx` next to every `{component}.tsx` in the same change that adds the component. How the story file is set up is in `testing/storybook/react/story-file-setup`.

**Why.** Components added without a story have no rendered example and no place for interaction tests, so their states are first seen in the running app and regressions in them go unnoticed.

**Correct:**

```text
features/projects/components/
├── project-card.tsx
├── project-card.stories.tsx
├── project-status-badge.tsx
└── project-status-badge.stories.tsx
```

## Keep each context with its provider and consumer hook in one name.context.tsx file

_medium · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Put each `React.createContext` call in its own `context/{name}.context.tsx` file, together with the provider component that supplies it and the consumer hook that reads it. Export the provider and the hook; keep the context object private to the file.

**Why.** A context split across files, or several contexts in one file, lets components read the raw context with `React.useContext` and skip the hook's missing-provider check, so a component rendered outside its provider silently gets the default value.

**Correct:**

```tsx
// context/filters.context.tsx
const FiltersContext = React.createContext<Filters | null>(null);

export function FiltersProvider({ filters, children }: FiltersProviderProps) {
  return <FiltersContext value={filters}>{children}</FiltersContext>;
}

export function useFilters() {
  const filters = React.useContext(FiltersContext);
  if (!filters) throw new Error("useFilters must be used inside FiltersProvider");
  return filters;
}
```

## Put a custom hook that creates no context in hooks/use-{name}.ts

_medium · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Put each custom hook that does not call `React.createContext` in `hooks/use-{name}.ts`: standalone client logic (state, effects, polling, subscriptions) or a hook that builds on a consumer hook from `context/`. A hook that exists to expose its own context lives in that context's `{name}.context.tsx`.

**Why.** Hooks defined inside component files or mixed with context files are hard to find and get copied instead of reused, so two components end up with diverging versions of the same polling or subscription logic.

**Correct:**

```tsx
// hooks/use-polling.ts
export function usePolling(url: string, intervalMs: number) {
  const [data, setData] = React.useState<JobStatus | null>(null);
  React.useEffect(() => { /* poll */ }, [url, intervalMs]);
  return data;
}
```

## Fix React Compiler lint diagnostics instead of switching the rules off

_medium · typescript, react, react-compiler_

**Rule.** Lint React code with the `recommended` preset of `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`, which includes the React Compiler rules, and run that lint in CI. Fix a compiler diagnostic in the code; do not set the rule to `off` or silence it with `eslint-disable`.

**Why.** When a component breaks a compiler rule the compiler skips it without failing the build, so the component silently loses its memoization and the reason is visible only in the lint output.

**Correct:**

```js
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";

export default defineConfig([reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended]);
```

## Import React as a namespace and reach every API through it

_medium · typescript, react_

**Rule.** Import React once per file as `import * as React from "react"` and call every export through the namespace (`React.useState`, `React.cache`, `React.useEffect`). Never use the default import or named imports from `"react"`.

**Why.** Mixed import styles make the same hook appear as `useState` in one file and `React.useState` in another, so searches miss call sites and every review re-litigates the style; the namespace form also needs no import edit when a file starts using another React API.

**Correct:**

```tsx
import * as React from "react";

const getUser = React.cache(fetchUser);

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```
